content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses identify sand's primary biblical meaning as an innumerable multitude (Abraham's descendants, peoples, armies — Gen 22:17; Hos 1:10; Heb 11:12; Rev 20:8), with a widely taught but separate alternative: sand as an unstable/foolish foundation in Matthew 7:26-27, plus minor senses (divine boundary of the sea, heaviness/burden). The multitude and foundation readings are treated as distinct, non-interacting meanings arising from different passages.","book_summary":"The book identifies sand as the countless multitude, and then derives the foundation image from that same identification: to build on the sand is to build on the crowd (the multitude of humanity) rather than on the covenant-rock. The two consensus meanings are fused into one symbol, with Matthew 7's sand reinterpreted as reliance on the mass of people rather than mere generic instability.","consensus_core_identification":"Sand = an innumerable multitude (primarily Abraham's promised descendants; also vast peoples/armies), with a separate, unrelated secondary sense of sand as an unstable foundation.","book_core_identification":"Sand = the countless multitude, and precisely because it is the multitude, it is a shifting foundation — building on sand means grounding oneself on the crowd instead of the covenant-rock.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book reclassifies the Matthew 7 foundation case. Consensus treats sand-as-foundation as a distinct symbol of instability/disobedience unconnected to the multitude sense; the book subsumes it under the multitude reading, so that the foolish builder's error is specifically trusting the crowd (popular opinion, the mass of humanity) rather than the covenant. The book thus rejects the consensus's view that the two senses 'coexist without conflict because they arise from different passages' (Response A) and merges them into a single symbolic logic.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book's central referent — countless multitude — is identical to the unanimous consensus primary meaning, so the core relation is EQUIVALENT and the verdict cannot be DIVERGENT or NOVEL. But the book materially changes the boundary of the symbol by folding the Matthew 7 foundation image into the multitude sense: sand is unstable because it is the crowd. This reclassifies a case the consensus assigns to a separate meaning (generic instability/foolish foundation) and gives it a new, more specific content (reliance on the multitude vs. the covenant-rock). That is a real interpretive change beyond wording, but it preserves the consensus category rather than replacing it, so REFINED is correct.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for MATCH: the book simply lists both consensus meanings (multitude and unstable foundation) in one sentence, and the 'crowd, not the covenant-rock' phrase is homiletic coloring rather than a material reclassification. Matthew 7 itself gives no textual warrant for reading its sand as 'the crowd,' so the fused reading may be too thin to count as a genuine boundary change; the cited verses on their face support only the two standard, separate senses.","confidence":"medium"}
